qAndA.answer: He explains that both his mother and father's families immigrated to the United States and that the United States' core history is an immigrant story.

qAndA.answer: He argues that pollution is essentially a subsidy and that there is a significant cost to inaction on climate change. He believes in a fundamental shift in the way the U.S. approaches its economic policy to account for these costs and advocate for a Green New Deal.

Legal training in the academic experience at law school was an extraordinary.

Enjoy your time when you guys get there.
It's a great place.
A great time in your life, too.

I went to Peace Corps.
So can you tell us more about your experience in there?
Yeah, so the Peace Corps for folks that don't know is a volunteer organization sponsored
by the United States government that has been operating for about 50 or so years longer than
that now.
And the goal on it is to provide opportunities for a broad swath of American citizens.
So a lot of folks are younger people who study at college.
But the oldest volunteers are actually in their 70s.
But to go back and serve their country by volunteering in communities of need overseas.
And there are literally dozens and dozens of countries that have requested that help from the United States.
I spent about two and a half years in the Dominican Republic.
And I loved it.
There's not a data that goes by that I don't draw on that experience in some way.
And I can tell you without question that I would not be sitting here before you as a member of Congress,
if not for that experience.
It got me well outside my comfort zone.
It got me to see the world of it differently.
You see the consequences of what happens when the work's and
when the challenges that people confront when they're not in a position to or
their ability to influence the trajectory of their own pathways is limited.
And you see what happens when there's not really a safety net there to catch people.
When there's not a healthcare system to fall back on.
When the education system doesn't actually make that guarantee that every child's going to have a chance to succeed.
And so it was a huge impact on my life.
As with anything that's that difficult, it doesn't mean you love every moment.
I didn't, but looking back on the experience there, it's certainly one that I hope quite dearly.
That's wonderful.
So in this Guizuara, there are many people here are immigrants for children and immigrants.
So that's an issue which is very close to the heart of this community.
So can you please explain to us your compassionate immigration policy and why that's so important to you?
Yeah, look, so I think a critical question for this time.
I think a critical question for a sick community, but a critical question for our country.
Because our country's story at its core is in fact, or should be an immigrant story.
Both of my, my family, my mother's side and my father's immigrated here to this country.
I'll be a long time apart.
But believing in the promise of this country, my mother's side for religious freedom, my father's side fleeing famine in Ireland many, many years ago.
And I consider myself an example of an immigrant story.
And what happens when you have a country that doesn't necessarily make it easy for an immigrant community in this country doesn't.
But that recognizes the contributions that an immigrant community can make to the foundation, the building box and the success of a nation.
And so when I see the actions of this administration and condoned, essentially, by our Republican party in the House and the Senate, it's awfully hard to justify.
And it's one of the reasons why I've been down to the border and a certain border a number of times participated in demonstrations and protests there.
Visited to customs and border patrol facilities have showed up at Logan Airport protesting their Muslim ban and amongst other acts and policies put forth by this administration.

Worked with lawyers and advocates on an individual case by case basis to try to make sure that folks have been caught up in the mess put forward by this, by this administration that the laws aren't in fact followed and the rights they are available to their rights.
Because I believe deeply in the contribution that immigrant community can make here.
Because I've seen that through my own family.
And I'm proud of their contribution.
And I think this country should be extremely proud of the fact that people from all over the world still want to come here.
And we should be terrified of the time when they don't, not the time when they do.
Right. So thank you for that.
You are a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee and as a member you are pushing to get the United States to re-enter the Paris agreement.
Yes.
So this is important because I want to make sure there's a planet for me to enjoy and for you guys to enjoy.
And I've got a two year old in the four year old.
I want to make sure they're able to enjoy it too.
And the fact is that the climate change is real.
The United States, our government can do something about it and we haven't.
And we haven't for a really long time.
But the last major piece of climate policy that was passed by Congress signed in a while by the president happened under Richard Nixon.
Under Richard Nixon when he passed the Clean Air Act.
It's been well over 40 years since that happened.
And you just can't wait any longer.
So yes, Paris is a critically important part of this.
But it's also why you got to go far beyond to the signing onto an international obligation.
We got to make that real.
You got to make those changes, those investments here in the United States now.
We needed to make them decades ago.
But you got to do it now.
You got to change the fundamental framework of our economy that accounts for the fact that pollution is a subsidy.
Somebody is damaging somebody is inflicting a cost on others not having to pay for it.
And you need to make sure that they're paying for it.
We need to make sure that people are held accountable for this.
And we got to, that's going to necessitate a fundamental shift in the way that we go about the framework to our economy.

And now we got to put our committees working on putting meat on the bones as to what that actually means.
Not just the important aspirational goals there, but how you actually play that out in policy.
And what is it going to take to build the political coalitions necessary to bring it across the finish line?
That's very true.
That's very true.
Now it's never too soon to, it's never too soon to ensure that your kids have a planet.
I mean, but that's what this is about, right?
Like you can't, you can't look at what is taking place today, whether it's forest fires across California or fires that envelop much of Australia.

Changing migration patterns, fishing patterns, etc.

We are seeing that cost today.

youtube_description:
Joseph Patrick Kennedy III is an American lawyer and politician serving as the U.S. Representative for Massachusetts's 4th congressional district since 2013. A member of the Democratic Party, he represents a congressional district that extends from the western suburbs of Boston to the state's South Coast. 

Nishkam TV is a first-ever online TV channel run by Sikh students in the USA with the mission of promoting interaction between different faiths and cultures to bring us closer as one humanity and enhance our lives. This TV channel will be run exclusively by students and will be available online on our website and on our YouTube (Nishkam TV), Facebook and Instagram social media channels.
